before.title: 4.0 Flat-Six Connecting Rod Defect – Recall (GTS 4.0 / Spyder)
before.description: Porsche issued a stop-sale and NHTSA safety recall 21V200000 (Porsche ref. AMA4) for naturally-aspirated 4.0L flat-six 718 models built with a defective batch of connecting rods. The rods may crack and loosen, which can lead to engine damage, an oil leak, or a sudden stall while driving, increasing the risk of a crash or fire. Roughly 190 vehicles globally were affected (about 20 already delivered to owners). Separately, the 4.0 community has documented sporadic catastrophic engine failures attributed to oil pump / oil supply issues on early-build (late-2020) cars, though Porsche has not issued an official statement tying failures to the oil pump.
before.solution: Check the VIN against NHTSA recall 21V200000 and confirm with a Porsche dealer that the connecting-rod remedy has been performed. Under the recall, dealers replace the connecting rods or the entire engine at no cost. For any 4.0 showing low oil pressure warnings or abnormal noise, stop driving and have it inspected immediately to avoid catastrophic damage.

before.title: Air-Oil Separator (AOS) Failure Causing Oil Ingestion and Smoke
before.description: The air-oil separator (crankcase breather/oil separator) on the turbocharged flat-four 718 can fail, causing excessive crankcase vacuum that draws engine oil into the intake. Owners report white/blue smoke (especially at startup or under acceleration), an oil smell, fouled spark plugs, and fuel-trim/check-engine faults. In severe cases the failing AOS has drawn paper-filter debris and oil that blocked the variable-cam (VarioCam) oil passages, requiring major engine teardown. Track-driven cars are especially prone because the stock unit cannot handle the load, risking oil ingestion that can hydro-lock or damage a cylinder.
before.solution: Diagnose with a crankcase-vacuum test; replace the failed AOS and clean the intake tract. Inspect spark plugs, oxygen sensors and MAF for oil contamination. For track use, consider an upgraded/baffled AOS or catch-can setup. Address promptly to prevent oil-ingestion damage to cams, pistons or sensors.
symptoms: White or blue smoke on startup/acceleration
Oil smell or oil residue in intake
Check engine light for fuel trim faults

before.title: Air-Oil Separator (AOS) Failure Causing Smoke and Misfires
before.description: The air-oil separator, which manages crankcase ventilation and returns oil vapor to the intake, can fail on the 718's flat-four. When the internal diaphragm tears, excessive crankcase vacuum draws engine oil into the intake tract, producing a characteristic thick cloud of white/blue smoke from the exhaust (most pronounced at startup and on acceleration), oil residue in the intake/throttle body, rough idle, misfires, and fuel-trim faults. A high-pitched whistle from the engine bay can accompany the increased crankcase pressure.
before.solution: Diagnose by checking for oil in the intake manifold/throttle body and measuring crankcase pressure. Replace the failed AOS (and clean oil residue from the intake tract); tracked cars may benefit from an upgraded separator. Clear fuel-trim and misfire codes after repair and verify the smoke and idle quality are resolved.
symptoms: White/blue smoke on startup and acceleration

before.title: Cooling System Changeover/Bypass Valve and Water Pump Failure Causing Overheating
before.description: The 718 Boxster's pressure-charged flat-four runs a complex cooling circuit with electrically actuated changeover (bypass) valves and a coolant-pump assembly that is prone to faults. Owners report an 'Engine over temp. Park vehicle to cool down' dashboard warning and erratic temperature-gauge behavior, often appearing after spirited driving or on hot days when the turbocharged engine demands extra cooling. Root causes include sticking/failing coolant changeover valves, a failing main water pump (early bearing wear, plastic-impeller degradation), and leaking coolant covers, sometimes escalating from a fault stored in the cooling-management module. This is distinct from coolant seepage at the turbo connections.
before.solution: Diagnose with the factory tool to identify whether the fault lies in the changeover valves, the water pump, or the coolant cover. Replace the failed changeover valve(s) and/or the water pump assembly and any cracked coolant cover, then bleed/refill the system per Porsche procedure. Because the plastic impeller and pump bearings wear early, many owners pre-emptively replace the water pump around 30,000-40,000 miles and inspect hoses, the expansion tank, and radiators at the same time.
symptoms: Engine over temp warning / park to cool down message
Whining or knocking from water pump

before.title: Fuel Collection Pipe / High-Pressure Fuel Line Leak (NHTSA Recall AH01 / 19V113)
before.description: Early 718 Boxster models were subject to a fuel-leak safety recall affecting the engine compartment. On certain 2017 cars, the fastening screws on the fuel collection pipes can shear off and allow fuel to leak in the engine compartment; in a related campaign, a luggage-compartment crossmember could detach in a crash and cause a fuel leak. A fuel leak in the presence of an ignition source raises the risk of fire. EU cars from the same period had an equivalent high-pressure fuel-pipe seal defect on cylinder bank 2 documented by European recall authorities.
before.solution: Check the VIN against open recalls (NHTSA campaign 19V113000 / Porsche reference AH01, and the EU bank-2 fuel-pipe seal recall). Dealers correct the fuel collection pipe fastening and secure the crossmember with additional rivets free of charge; the EU campaign replaces/reseals the affected high-pressure fuel pipe. Repairs are performed at no cost under the recall.

proposal.title: Fuel Collection Pipe / High-Pressure Fuel Line Leak (NHTSA Recall AH01 / 19V113)
proposal.description: The title conflates two separate recalls. Campaign 17V-054/Porsche AH01 covers certain 2017 718 Boxster vehicles whose fuel-collection-pipe fastening screws may shear and allow a high-pressure fuel leak. Campaign 19V-113/Porsche AKA3 covers 2017-2019 cars whose luggage-compartment crossmember may detach in a crash and possibly cause a fuel leak. AH01 is not campaign 19V-113, and the second condition is not a high-pressure collection-pipe leak.

Check the VIN separately against 17V-054/AH01 and 19V-113/AKA3 and confirm current remedy availability and charge with Porsche. Do not buy a fuel rail, screws, line or crossmember from this page; the applicable campaign, leak path, part number and VIN fitment must be established first.

before.title: Gasoline Particulate Filter (OPF/GPF) Clogging and Failure
before.description: European-spec 718 Boxster models (which run an active gasoline/Otto particulate filter, unlike US-spec cars where the filter is largely inactive) suffer premature GPF clogging and failure. Owners report the check-engine light appearing without any prior prompt to perform an active regeneration, sometimes accompanied by reduced power or limp mode. Forum investigations point strongly to a software/regeneration-strategy fault and faulty differential-pressure sensor readings rather than genuine physical filter saturation, but Porsche has classified blocked filters as resulting from upstream issues and has frequently denied warranty/extended-warranty coverage, leaving owners facing very large bills. Most reported on 2019-2020 EU cars with the 2.0L and 2.5L turbo engines.
before.solution: Have a dealer or Porsche specialist read the differential-pressure data and confirm whether the filter is genuinely saturated or the sensor is misreading before authorizing replacement. Force an active/service regeneration and apply the latest engine-control and GPF software updates, which have resolved many cases. Avoid repeated short, low-temperature trips and use quality fuel to promote passive regeneration. If the filter is genuinely failed, the combined GPF/catalytic-converter unit must be replaced; open a case with Porsche Customer Care to pursue goodwill coverage given the documented software involvement.
symptoms: Check engine light with no regeneration prompt

before.title: Gasoline Particulate Filter (GPF/OPF) Clogging and Premature Failure
before.description: EU-spec (and later global) 718 four-cylinder cars fitted with a gasoline particulate filter (German: Ottopartikelfilter/OPF) have suffered premature clogging and outright filter failure. Owners report engine-management warning lights, restricted performance/limp mode, and increased fuel consumption. The CAN-bus-monitored exhaust flap/sensor setup can trigger a fault and limp mode if not detected. Documented EU cases include a 2019 Cayman 718 needing GPF replacement at only ~17,000 miles, with quotes around £5,800+VAT, often disputed under warranty because filters are excluded as wear items. Short-trip driving (which prevents passive regeneration) and incorrect-spec oil (e.g. A40 instead of the required C-spec low-ash oil) accelerate the problem. The OPF also reportedly increases turbo lag and restricts the engine on so-equipped cars.
before.solution: Drive the car periodically at sustained highway speed/load to allow the GPF to passively regenerate; avoid repeated short trips. Use only the manufacturer-specified low-ash (C-spec) engine oil. If limp mode or a GPF fault appears, scan for codes and have the filter/differential-pressure sensor inspected; a clogged filter may require forced regeneration or replacement. Pursue a goodwill/warranty claim for premature (low-mileage) failures.

before.title: Manual Transmission 1st-to-2nd Gear Synchro Grind
before.description: Owners of the 6-speed manual 718 Boxster report a grinding/balking sensation when shifting from 1st to 2nd gear, particularly during cooler, low-rpm shifts before the gearbox warms up. The 2nd-gear synchro is most affected; the grind rarely occurs above roughly 3,300 rpm or between other gear pairs. Contributing factors include the clutch not fully disengaging (commonly air in the hydraulic clutch line causing clutch drag), worn 2nd-gear synchros, and the notchy cold-shift character of these gearboxes. Persistent grinding accelerates synchro wear.
before.solution: Bleed the clutch hydraulic system to remove air and ensure full disengagement, and verify clutch pedal travel/master-cylinder operation. Use the correct Porsche manual-transmission fluid and allow the gearbox to warm before brisk shifting. If the synchro is already damaged, the transmission must be opened to replace the 2nd-gear synchro assembly; some cars have been addressed under warranty.

before.title: Oil Leaks from Rear Main Seal, Valve Cover and Spark Plug Tube Seals
before.description: As the 718 ages and heat-cycles, multiple engine seals tend to weep oil. Common leak points are the rear main seal (RMS, between engine and transmission), the valve cover gaskets, and the spark plug tube seals. Symptoms include an oily film/drips under the car, oil residue on the spark plugs and ignition coils, and a burning-oil smell. Oil on the plugs/coils can eventually cause misfires. The rear main seal in particular is a well-known Porsche flat-engine weak point (carried over from earlier Boxster/Cayman/996/997 platforms) and is labor-intensive because transmission removal is required to access it.
before.solution: Clean suspected areas, then short-drive and re-inspect to pinpoint the source. Valve-cover and spark-plug-tube seals are the easiest to address and should be done at major services. A confirmed rear main seal leak requires transmission removal — often combined with a clutch job on manual cars to save labor. Also check oil cooler and cam seals as secondary culprits.
symptoms: Oil drips or oily film under the car
Oil residue on spark plugs and coils
Smoke from oil on hot exhaust

before.title: Rear Main Seal and Engine Oil Seal Leaks
before.description: As the turbocharged flat-four ages and is subjected to high underbody heat, the engine's oil seals degrade and weep oil. The most significant is the rear main seal between the engine and transmission, which produces an oily film and drips at the bellhousing area; valve-cover gaskets and spark-plug-tube seals also leak, allowing oil onto the ignition coils and plugs. Left unaddressed, oil-soaked coils cause misfires, and oil contamination of wiring and hot exhaust components creates a smell and a small fire risk.
before.solution: Confirm the leak source (rear main seal vs. valve cover vs. spark-plug tubes) since they look similar from underneath. Replace the rear main seal during a clutch or transmission-removal service to save labor, and renew valve-cover gaskets and spark-plug-tube seals with high-quality parts when oil is found on the plugs/coils. Clean affected ignition components and inspect coils for oil damage. Address any oil found on plugs immediately to prevent misfires.

before.title: Water Pump Bearing and Impeller Failure (Flat-Four 2.0/2.5)
before.description: The engine-driven coolant pump on the turbocharged flat-four 718 (shared design lineage with the 991.2 911) is a known weak point. The pump's bearing wears prematurely and the plastic impeller can degrade or shed, leading to coolant leaks, whining/knocking noise from the pump, and erratic coolant temperature behavior. A failing internal seal can also draw coolant into the engine's vacuum/changeover-valve circuit during warmup. Many owners report failures or proactive replacement around 30,000-40,000 miles (roughly 50,000-65,000 km), well before a coolant pump should normally need service. This is mechanically distinct from external coolant leaks at the turbo connections.
before.solution: Inspect the water pump for weeping/bearing play and listen for whine; replace the pump (often with the thermostat) proactively at around 30k-40k miles or at the first sign of a leak/noise. Confirm coolant is not being pulled into the vacuum/changeover-valve system. Use only Porsche-approved coolant and bleed the system properly after replacement to avoid air pockets and overheating.
symptoms: Pink or orange coolant puddle under engine
Whining or knocking noise from pump
Erratic or rising coolant temperature gauge
